meta.title: Binary decision diagrams: compressing truth tables
meta.tools: Own reduced ordered BDD package (unique table, memoised ITE/apply), node counts vs truth-table size, variable-ordering experiments on an n-bit comparator and adder, the hidden-weighted-bit and multiplier hard cases
meta.summary: Build ROBDDs from scratch and measure how compactly they represent useful functions: linear size for adders and comparators with a good variable order, exponential with a bad one, and exponential regardless of order for multiplication — the facts that shaped formal verification.
meta.problem: A 64-input function has 2⁶⁴ truth-table rows. How can a verification tool still reason about it exactly?
meta.theory:
An ROBDD (fixed variable order, merged isomorphic subgraphs, no redundant tests) is canonical: two functions are equal iff their BDDs are identical nodes. Size depends dramatically on order: for the comparator $\bigwedge(a_i = b_i)$ the interleaved order
a₁b₁a₂b₂… needs 3n + 2 nodes, the separated order a₁…a_nb₁…b_n needs 3·2ⁿ − 1. The carry-out of an n-bit adder is linear when interleaved. Multiplier outputs need exponential BDDs for *every* order (Bryant 1991).
meta.method:
Node counts (including the two terminals) for n = 2…10: equality comparator under both orders, adder carry-out (interleaved), middle output bit of an n×n multiplier (n ≤ 7, interleaved). Canonicity test: two structurally different expressions of the
same function must return the identical node.

rows.quantity: Canonicity: AB + A'C and AB + A'C + BC reduce to the identical node (1 = yes)
Adder carry-out, interleaved: linear growth (nodes per extra bit)
Multiplier middle bit: node count grows exponentially (log₂ growth per bit > 0.5)
